key_terms.meaning: A small computer that reads sensors and drives actuators; it replaced mechanical control in engines, brakes and body systems.
Stepped emission limits for new vehicles; India followed the Euro steps a few years later and went from BS IV to BS VI in 2020.
Charge put into the battery by the alternator minus charge taken out by the loads over a trip; it must stay positive.
A = (I × ρ × l) ÷ ΔU, with ρ = 0.0172 Ω·mm²/m for copper; round up to the next standard size.
Battery positive (always live), ignition-switched positive, ground, starter control (DIN 72552).
Working properly in the electrical noise of other parts (immunity) without making too much noise (emission).
A diode across a relay or solenoid coil that carries the coil current at switch-off, clamping the spike to about 0.7 V above supply.
Lead dioxide (PbO₂) on the positive plate and spongy lead (Pb) on the negative plate; it takes part in the reaction.
Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ ⇌ 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O (discharge to the right, charge to the left).
Electrolyte density ÷ water density; about 1.28 full and 1.12 flat. Cell voltage ≈ SG + 0.84.
Charge delivered at the 20 h rate to 10.5 V: Ah = I × t; a 60 Ah battery gives 3 A for 20 h.
Current a 12 V battery delivers for 30 s at −18 °C while staying at or above 7.2 V (SAE).
Minutes a full battery supplies 25 A at about 25 °C before falling to 10.5 V.
A lead-calcium battery with so little water loss that it needs no topping-up; flooded versions are vented, VRLA versions have a valve.
The first field current at key-on, through the charge warning lamp into D+; exciter diodes take over once the alternator runs.
f = (p × N) ÷ 120, with p rotor poles and N alternator rpm; ripple of the bridge output is 6f.
Alternator speed at which it reaches the set voltage without delivering current (cut-in); about 1000 rpm.
I ≈ I_max(1 − n₀ ÷ n): emf and stator reactance both grow with speed, so output current levels off.
The regulator switches the field with duty cycle D; average field current I_f ≈ D × V_bus ÷ R_f.
η = P_out ÷ P_in × 100 %; losses are copper, iron, diode (2 × V_F × I_dc), brush, bearing and fan.
P = Tω with ω = 2πN ÷ 60; zero at stall even though torque is highest there.
Lowest cranking speed for reliable first firing: about 60–100 rpm for petrol engines and 100–200 rpm for diesels.
Solenoid coils: together about 40 A to pull the plunger; the main contacts then short the pull-in coil and about 10 A holds it.
One-way roller clutch in the pinion so the running engine cannot drive the starter armature.
Above the normal load current and at or below the current the wire can carry; the fuse protects the wire.
A resistor path that charges the inverter capacitors before the main contactor closes, so inrush cannot weld it.

takeaways: Vehicle electrics grew from a few lamps and an ignition coil into networked control because loads, emission laws and safety rules kept rising; 12 V and the alternator came first, ECUs and CAN later.
The power supply is a generator, a store and grouped loads on one bus; the charge balance over a trip decides whether the battery stays charged.
A wire is sized by A = Iρl ÷ ΔU, rounded up to a standard size and checked for temperature; a fuse is chosen to protect that wire.
EMC has a source, a path and a sink: suppress at the source (diodes, capacitors, resistor plugs), block the path (short, twisted, screened wires, ground straps) and harden the sink.
A 12 V battery is six lead-acid cells of about 2.1 V; discharge turns both plates to lead sulfate and uses acid, so specific gravity and rest voltage show the state of charge.
Ah, reserve capacity and CCA answer different questions; load, conductance and open-circuit tests show the real condition, and a replacement must match the technology.
The alternator makes three-phase AC rectified by six diodes; its current is zero below n₀ and limits itself at high speed, so idle speed and pulley ratio decide the charge balance in traffic.
The regulator holds the bus voltage by switching the field; the diodes are usually the largest single loss.
A starter must reach the minimum starting speed at the meeting point of its torque curve and the engine resistance; cold and voltage drop both pull that point down.
A small key current works a relay and the solenoid, which mesh the pinion before closing the 250 A main contacts; the ignition secondary and EV traction voltage are separate high-voltage domains.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit usually ask for a labelled sketch plus a working explanation: plan every answer round a construction or circuit diagram and a step-by-step current or energy path, then add the rating numbers. Most syllabi now add vehicle power supply, wire sizing and EMC to batteries, charging and starting, so expect one question on them.

bank.q: Trace the evolution of automotive electronics from simple ignition and lighting loads to networked control. Name the pressure that forced each step.
outline: Early loads: ignition, lamps; magneto and hand crank
Electric starter and battery-coil ignition; 6 V to 12 V; dynamo to alternator, driven by growing loads
Emission laws (Euro and Bharat Stage steps) force electronic ignition, fuel injection and ECUs with oxygen feedback
Safety and comfort: ABS, airbags, ESP, ADAS
Many ECUs share a data bus (CAN) and on-board diagnostics
Result: distributed electronic control, 48 V and EV domains
answer: Start with the early car (before about 1912). The engine was cranked by hand and a magneto, a small engine-driven generator, made the spark. Lamps were few, so the only essential electrical load was ignition and a battery was optional.

Pressure 1, convenience and safety of starting. In 1912 the electric self-starter (designed by Charles Kettering for Cadillac) replaced the crank. A starter needs a rechargeable battery, so the battery, a belt-driven dynamo and battery-coil ignition became standard.

answer.text: Pressure 2, growing electrical loads. Lamps, wipers, heaters and radios raised the current. From the mid-1950s makers moved from 6 V to 12 V. For the same power the current halves, and the cable loss falls to a quarter. With 300 W of load and 0.01 Ω of cable:

answer: Pressure 3, output at idle. The dynamo, with its commutator, gave little current at low speed. From 1960 the alternator, a three-phase machine with a diode rectifier, replaced it: it charges at idle and spins faster without commutator wear. With a 14.0 V bus, a 35 A dynamo gives 490 W while a modern 120 A alternator gives 1680 W, about 3.4 times as much.

answer.text: Pressure 4, emission laws. From the 1970s, and in Europe with the Euro stages from 1992, limits on CO, HC and NOx required a three-way catalyst, which works only near the chemically correct air-fuel ratio. A carburettor cannot hold that ratio, so electronic fuel injection with an ECU and an oxygen-sensor feedback loop replaced it, and electronic ignition replaced contact points. India followed with Bharat Stage norms:

answer: Pressure 5, safety and comfort. Anti-lock braking, airbags, electronic stability control and later ADAS (adaptive cruise, emergency braking) need fast sensing, calculation and actuation, which only electronics can give.

Pressure 6, wiring weight and diagnosis. Separate wires for every signal between many ECUs became heavy and hard to diagnose. The CAN bus (developed in the 1980s, first used in a production car in 1991) lets many ECUs share two wires, and OBD-II diagnostics run over it; CAN became the required OBD-II protocol for new US cars from the 2008 model year.

Draw the chain as a timeline: hand crank and magneto → self-starter and battery ignition (1912) → 12 V (1950s) → alternator (1960) → electronic ignition (1970s) → fuel injection and ECU (1980s) → CAN (1991) → ADAS, 48 V and EV (2010s), with the pressure written under each group: loads, emission laws, safety and networking.

Conclude: each step solved a load or a legal problem and made the next possible, so a modern car is a network of ECUs on a regulated 14 V bus, and electric vehicles add a separate high-voltage domain. Check: the three pressures named (loads, emissions, safety) account for every step on the timeline.

bank.q: Explain the electrical power supply of a conventional vehicle: generator, store and loads, the charge balance, single- and two-battery systems, and the way circuit diagrams and terminal numbers show it.
outline: Alternator generates, battery stores, loads consume, all on one bus with chassis return
Load groups: permanent, continuous, long-time, short-time
Charge balance with a numerical example
Single battery; two-battery systems; 24 V in trucks
Circuit, wiring, terminal and location diagrams; DIN 72552 terminals 30, 15, 31, 50, 85/86, 87
answer: Parts of the supply: the alternator generates energy while the engine runs; the battery stores energy for starting and for any deficit; the loads (consumers) use it. All are joined on one 12 V bus, with the return through the body and engine block (terminal 31).

Load groups, by how long they draw current: permanent loads (clock, alarm, ECU standby, milliamperes all the time); continuous loads that run with the engine (ignition, injection, fuel pump); long-time loads (lamps, blower, rear-window heater, wipers, radio); short-time loads (starter, horn, power windows). The groups decide how much charge each takes from the battery.

answer.text: Charge balance: charge in from the alternator minus charge out to the loads over a trip. Worked case: at night in slow traffic the loads total 59.2 A and the alternator at idle gives 45 A.
answer.pre:
battery current = 59.2 − 45 = 14.2 A (discharge)
charge lost in 30 min = 14.2 A × 0.5 h = 7.1 Ah
charge to put back = 7.1 × 1.1 = 7.8 Ah
highway surplus = 90 − 59.2 = 30.8 A
recharge time = 7.8 ÷ 30.8 = 0.25 h ≈ 15 min

answer: So the balance is positive only if the highway part of the trip lasts at least about 15 minutes; many short trips in traffic give a negative balance and a flat battery.

Single and two-battery systems: most cars use one 12 V battery. Vehicles with heavy accessory or standby loads (ambulances, caravans, buses) use a starter battery for cranking and a supply battery for the loads, joined through a relay or isolator so the loads cannot drain the starter battery. Heavy trucks use 24 V, two 12 V batteries in series, which halves the current for the same power.

Diagrams: a circuit diagram draws each current path as a straight line from the supply at the top (30 or 15) to ground (31) at the bottom, placing parts for clarity; a wiring diagram shows real positions, harness routes, wire colours and sizes (for example 1.5 RD/WH: 1.5 mm², red with a white stripe); a terminal diagram lists connector pins; a location diagram shows where parts are fitted.

answer.text: Terminal numbers (DIN 72552) are stamped on the parts:

head: Terminal
Meaning
rows: relay contact input, normally open, normally closed

answer: Sketch: battery and alternator on the bus, the distribution box with fuses, one relay-switched load (switch on 15 → coil 86-85; contact 30-87 → load → 31). Check: every load in the sketch has a fuse on its feed and returns to 31.

bank.q: Explain electromagnetic compatibility in a vehicle: the sources of interference, the coupling paths and the suppression measures. Work one numerical example.
outline: EMC = emission + immunity; source → path → sink
Sources: ignition, commutator motors, coils, alternator, load dump; external transmitters
Paths: conducted, capacitive (dv/dt), inductive (di/dt), radiated
Suppression at source, on the path, at the sink; test standards
Example: relay coil with freewheeling diode, or an LC filter
answer: Definition: electromagnetic compatibility is the ability of each electrical part to work properly in the vehicle's electromagnetic surroundings (immunity) without disturbing other parts or receivers (emission). Every problem has a source, a coupling path and a sink.

Sources inside the vehicle: the ignition spark, a very fast current pulse that radiates up to hundreds of megahertz; commutator motors (wipers, blower, fan) whose brushes spark; the alternator diodes; relays, solenoids and injectors, which give spikes when switched off; PWM drivers; and the load dump, a surge of around a hundred volts for a few hundred milliseconds when the battery is disconnected while the alternator charges. Outside: broadcast and mobile transmitters, radar, electrostatic discharge.
Sinks: radio and GPS receivers, ECU inputs, sensor lines and data buses.

Coupling paths: conducted (two circuits share a wire or ground point, so a noisy current's drop appears in the quiet circuit); capacitive (a fast voltage change pushes current into a neighbouring wire, growing with dv/dt); inductive (a changing current's magnetic field induces a voltage in nearby loops, growing with di/dt and loop area); radiated (a wire about a quarter wavelength long, 75 cm at 100 MHz, acts as an aerial).

Suppression at the source: freewheeling diodes, RC networks or varistors across coils; capacitors at motor brushes and alternator B+; chokes; resistor spark plugs and suppression caps or leads; Zener rectifier diodes to clamp the load dump. On the path: short routes, power and signal wires apart, twisted pairs (CAN), screened cables, short wide ground straps between engine, body and exhaust, one clean ground point for sensors. At the sink: filters and ferrites on ECU inputs, metal housings, plausibility checks in software.

answer.text: Numerical example, relay coil (R = 85  Ω, L = 0.20 H, 12 V):
answer.pre:
I = 12 ÷ 85 = 0.141 A
stored energy W = ½LI² = 0.5 × 0.20 × 0.141² = 2.0 mJ
without suppression, stopping I in 2 µs: V = L di/dt = 0.20 × 0.141 ÷ 2×10⁻⁶ ≈ 14 kV
with a freewheeling diode: coil clamped at 0.7 V, transistor sees 12.7 V
decay τ = L ÷ R = 0.20 ÷ 85 = 2.35 ms; to 10 % in τ ln 10 = 5.4 ms

answer.text: Second example, LC filter on a fan motor (5 µH, 1 µF):
answer.pre:
f<sub>c</sub> = 1 ÷ (2π√(LC)) = 1 ÷ (2π × 2.236×10⁻⁶) = 71.2 kHz
at 1 MHz: X<sub>L</sub> = 31.4 Ω (series), X<sub>C</sub> = 0.159 Ω (to ground)
attenuation ≈ 40 dB × log₁₀(1 MHz ÷ 71.2 kHz) = 40 × 1.148 = 45.9 dB (about 200 times)

answer: Testing: components are measured on a bench to CISPR 25 radio-emission limits and conducted transients to ISO 7637-2; immunity to fields is tested to the ISO 11452 series; the whole vehicle is tested in a screened, absorber-lined room.

Sketch the three columns (source, path, sink) with one remedy under each. Check: the diode example shows why every relay coil driven by an ECU transistor needs suppression, since 14 kV against 12.7 V is the difference between a destroyed and a safe transistor.

bank.q: Draw the construction of a lead-acid cell and explain the reactions during discharge and recharge. Show how the electrolyte indicates the state of charge.
outline: Positive plate PbO₂, negative spongy Pb, on lead-alloy grids; separators; electrolyte; case with six cells, straps, connectors, vents
Electrode and overall reactions on discharge
Charging reverses them; gassing above 2.3–2.4 V per cell
SG falls as acid is used; cell V ≈ SG + 0.84; 3.66 g acid per Ah
Faults: sulfation, stratification, self-discharge
answer: Sketch: a polypropylene case divided into six cells; in each cell alternating positive and negative plates with porous separators between them, plates of one polarity welded to a strap, the straps rising to the + and − posts (the positive post is larger), cell connectors through the partitions, the electrolyte above the plates and vent caps on the cover.

Plates: each plate is a cast lead-alloy grid that carries current and holds the active material. The positive active material is lead dioxide, PbO₂ (dark brown); the negative is spongy lead, Pb (grey, porous). Pasted plates (paste of lead oxides on the grid, then formed by charging) are used in vehicles; Planté plates, formed from solid lead, are thick, long-lived and suit standby use.
Separators of polyethylene, glass fibre or rubber let ions pass but stop the plates touching. The electrolyte is dilute sulfuric acid, specific gravity about 1.28 when fully charged.

answer.text: Discharge reactions:
answer.pre:
negative plate:  Pb + HSO₄⁻ → PbSO₄ + H⁺ + 2e⁻        (oxidation)
positive plate:  PbO₂ + HSO₄⁻ + 3H⁺ + 2e⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2H₂O   (reduction)
overall:         Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O

answer: Both plates turn to lead sulfate, and the acid is used while water is formed, so the electrolyte gets weaker. Electrons leave the negative plate through the external circuit to the positive plate.

Charging: an external voltage above the battery's (the charging system holds about 13.8–14.4 V) drives current the other way, so every reaction runs backwards: 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O → Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄. The positive plate stays positive. Above about 2.3–2.4 V per cell the current starts splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen (gassing), which loses water and makes an explosive gas.

answer.text: State of charge from the electrolyte: the rested cell voltage is about SG + 0.84, and each ampere-hour uses 3600 C ÷ 96,485 C/mol = 0.0373 mol of H₂SO₄ = 3.66 g.

answer: Example: after 30 Ah each cell has used 30 × 3.66 = 110 g of acid, 659 g in the six cells, which is why a hydrometer reading falls.

Faults that age a battery: sulfation (lead sulfate left standing hardens and no longer converts back), stratification (dense acid settles at the bottom), self-discharge (a few per cent a month, faster when warm), and shedding of active material. Check: 6 × 2.1 V = 12.6 V matches the rested voltage between the full and half rows of the table.

bank.q: Define ampere-hour rating, cold cranking amps and reserve capacity. Give values for a typical car battery and explain why each rating suits a different job.
outline: Ah at the 20 h rate to 10.5 V; I = Ah ÷ 20
CCA at −18 °C, 30 s, at least 7.2 V
RC at 25 A, about 25 °C, to 10.5 V, in minutes
Typical 60 Ah, CCA 450 A, RC 100 min
Which rating for a hot coastal city and which for a cold hill town
answer: Ampere-hour (Ah) rating: the charge a fully charged battery delivers at a constant current over 20 h, at about 25 °C, before its voltage falls to 10.5 V (1.75 V per cell). Ah = I × t. A 60 Ah battery is tested at I = 60 ÷ 20 = 3 A.

Cold cranking amps (CCA): the current the battery delivers for 30 s at −18 °C while its terminal voltage stays at or above 7.2 V (SAE definition). It measures cold-start strength: high current from a cold battery whose acid and plates are sluggish. Cranking amps (CA) is the same test at 0 °C.
Reserve capacity (RC): the minutes a fully charged battery at about 25 °C supplies 25 A before falling to 10.5 V. It answers how long the car can run its essential loads if the alternator fails.

answer.text: Typical car battery and what the numbers mean:

head: Rating
Typical value
What it gives
rows: 25 A × 100 ÷ 60 h = 41.7 Ah at the 25 A rate

answer: The 41.7 Ah from the reserve test is less than 60 Ah because at the higher current the acid cannot reach the inner pores of the plates in time, so the same battery gives fewer ampere-hours at a faster rate. That is why each rating names its test conditions.

Why each suits a different job: Ah tells how much charge is stored for long, low-current use (standby loads, accessories with the engine off); RC tells how long the vehicle survives an alternator failure; CCA tells whether the battery can crank a cold engine. A battery with a high Ah can still have a low CCA if its plates are fewer or thicker, because cranking current depends on plate area and internal resistance.

Choice by climate: in a hot coastal city cold cranking is easy, but heat speeds water loss and grid corrosion, so compare RC and choose a maintenance-free type; in a cold hill town compare CCA first, because cold oil raises cranking torque while the cold battery gives less current.
Check: 450 A at 7.2 V is 3240 W for 30 s; a 60 Ah rating at 3 A and 12 V average is only 36 W. The two ratings describe very different duties, which is the point of the question.

bank.q: Explain the charging circuit from alternator to battery, including the path through the warning lamp, the exciter diodes and the voltage-sense wire.
outline: Alternator B+ through the fused cable to battery and loads; body return
Key-on: battery → ignition switch → lamp → D+ → field → regulator → ground; lamp lit
Running: exciter diodes feed D+; lamp has equal voltage on both sides and goes out
Regulator controls field current from sensed voltage
Sense wire and voltage drop example
answer: Main path: the alternator's six power diodes deliver DC at B+. A thick cable, protected by a fuse or fusible link, runs from B+ to the battery positive and the distribution box. The return is through the body and engine block to battery negative.

Key-on, engine stopped: battery positive → ignition switch (terminal 15) → charge warning lamp → alternator D+ → regulator → field winding → ground. This small current is the pre-excitation: it gives the rotor a weak magnetic field so the alternator can start generating. The lamp lights because current flows through it.

Engine running: the stator generates, and three exciter diodes (the diode trio) feed D+ from the stator phases. D+ rises to about bus voltage, so both ends of the lamp sit near 14 V; the lamp current falls to almost zero and the lamp goes out. A lamp that stays on or glows shows that D+ is below battery voltage: the alternator is not charging.

Regulation: the regulator compares the sensed voltage with its set point (about 13.8–14.4 V) and switches the field current; more field gives more output. It controls voltage, not current; the charging current follows from the difference between the bus and the battery's rest voltage.

answer.text: Charging current at the start: with the bus at 14.2 V, a battery at rest at 12.4 V and an internal resistance of 0.02 Ω:
answer.pre:
I = (14.2 − 12.4) ÷ 0.02 = 1.8 ÷ 0.02 = 90 A (if the alternator can supply it)
the current falls as the battery charges and its rest voltage rises

answer.text: Sense wire: if the regulator senses at B+, any drop in the charging cable reaches the battery. Cable 1.2 m of 10 mm² with a corroded joint of 0.004 Ω at 80 A:
answer.pre:
cable R = 0.0172 × 1.2 ÷ 10 = 0.00206 Ω
with joint: R = 0.00606 Ω, drop = 80 × 0.00606 = 0.485 V → battery gets 13.7 V
clean: drop = 80 × 0.00206 = 0.165 V → battery gets 14.0 V

answer: A separate sense wire to the battery carries almost no current, so it reports the true battery voltage and the regulator raises B+ (here to about 14.7 V) until the battery sees the set point. Sketch the circuit: alternator box (stator, power diodes, exciter diodes, regulator, field), B+ cable to battery and loads, key and lamp to D+, dashed sense wire. Check: a failed lamp with no parallel resistor removes pre-excitation, which is why some alternators will not charge with a blown warning bulb.

bank.q: Describe the construction of a claw-pole alternator with a labelled sketch and explain how three-phase output is produced and rectified. Find the stator frequency for a 12-pole rotor at 6000 rpm.
outline: Rotor: field coil, interleaved claw poles, slip rings and brushes
Stator: three-phase winding in a laminated core
Faraday and Lenz; phases 120° apart; f = pN ÷ 120
Six-diode bridge, V_dc ≈ 1.35 V_LL, ripple 6f; exciter diodes
Fans, housing, pulley ratio; versions
answer: Sketch: drive-end and slip-ring-end housings with bearings; the rotor on the shaft with one field coil enclosed by two interleaved claw-shaped pole pieces; two slip rings and the brush holder with the regulator; the stator core round the rotor with three windings; the rectifier plate with diodes; internal fans; the belt pulley.

Rotor: a single field coil wound round the shaft carries DC from the brushes and slip rings. The two claw pole pieces interlock, so the claws become alternate north and south poles, typically 12 poles (6 pairs), giving a strong field from a simple, cheap rotor. Only the small field current (a few amperes) passes the brushes.

Stator: a laminated steel core (laminations cut eddy-current loss) with three windings in slots, placed 120 electrical degrees apart, usually star-connected. The output current flows in these stationary windings, so it needs no sliding contacts.

Principle: Faraday's law, e = −N dΦ/dt. As the rotor turns, the alternating poles sweep past each stator coil and the flux through it reverses, inducing an alternating emf; the three phases are 120° apart. The minus sign (Lenz's law) means the induced current opposes the change, so the belt must supply mechanical power for every watt delivered.

answer.text: Frequency for p = 12 poles at N = 6000 rpm:

Rectification: six power diodes form a three-phase bridge, three to B+ and three to ground; at any instant the pair connected to the most positive and the most negative phase conducts, so two diodes are always in series. The average output of an ideal bridge is V_dc ≈ 1.35 V_LL. To give 14.0 V after two diode drops of 0.9 V:
answer.pre: 1.35 V<sub>LL</sub> = 14.0 + 2 × 0.9 = 15.8 V  →  V<sub>LL</sub> = 15.8 ÷ 1.35 = 11.7 V RMS line-to-line

answer: Three smaller exciter diodes feed D+ and the field; in many alternators the power diodes are Zener types that clamp voltage surges. Two internal fans pull air through the housing, and the pulley is smaller than the crank pulley (ratio about 2.5 to 3) so the alternator runs fast enough to charge at idle.

Versions: compact claw-pole alternators with internal fans (cars), liquid-cooled versions, and brushless (windingless-rotor) versions for long-running commercial vehicles. Check: 600 Hz at 6000 rpm is 0.1 Hz per rpm for 12 poles, so at an idle speed of 2000 rpm the stator runs at 200 Hz.

bank.q: List the requirements of a starting system for an IC engine and explain each in one or two lines, with numbers where you can.
outline: Cranking torque above compression and friction, cold
Cranking speed above minimum starting speed (petrol 60–100, diesel 100–200 rpm)
Cranking power P = Tω
Battery and cable able to hold voltage under hundreds of amperes
Engagement before power and disengagement after firing; one-way clutch
Short duty, small control current
answer: Torque: the starter must overcome compression of the next cylinder, ring, bearing and valve-train friction and pumping, which are largest in a cold engine with thick oil. A diesel, with a compression ratio of 16:1 to 22:1 against 8:1 to 12:1 for petrol, needs much more torque.

Speed: the engine must be turned above its minimum starting speed, about 60–100 rpm for a petrol engine and 100–200 rpm for a diesel, which must reach self-ignition temperature by compression alone. Below this, gas leaks past the rings and heat is lost to cold walls.

answer.text: Power: torque and speed together. For 45 N·m at 200 rpm:

answer: Stable cranking point: the starter torque falls with speed and the engine resistance rises; the engine settles where they meet, and that point must lie above the minimum starting speed at the coldest expected temperature.

Electrical supply: the battery must deliver a few hundred amperes with little voltage sag (V = E − IR; 300 A through 0.01 Ω loses 3 V), so CCA, cable size and clean terminals are part of the starting system.

Engagement: the pinion must mesh with the ring gear before full power is applied (pre-engaged drive) and must not be driven by the running engine (overrunning clutch), then return when the key is released.

Gear ratio: a small fast motor drives the engine through the pinion and ring gear, typically 10:1 to 15:1. With 12 teeth on the pinion and 132 on the ring gear the ratio is 11:1, so 200 rpm at the crankshaft needs 2200 rpm at the armature and only 45 ÷ 11 = 4.1 N·m from the motor (ignoring gear losses).

Control and duty: the key must switch only a small current (relay and solenoid), and the starter is rated for short duty: a few seconds of cranking with rests between attempts, because the armature heats quickly at several hundred amperes.

Size, cost and life: the starter must be small and light enough to fit beside the gearbox, cheap, sealed against water and dirt, and able to do tens of thousands of starts; a stop-start car may need several hundred thousand, which is why such cars use a reinforced starter or a belt starter-generator.

Check: the list covers torque, speed, power, gear ratio, supply, engagement, control and duty, and size and life. The numbers agree: 942 W at the crankshaft is 4.1 N·m × 2200 rpm at the armature (4.1 × 2π × 2200 ÷ 60 = 945 W, the small difference coming from rounding 4.1).

bank.q: An alternator has a zero-ampere speed of 1000 rpm and a rated current of 120 A at 6000 rpm, and follows I = I_max(1 − n₀ ÷ n). The pulley ratio is 2.5 and the engine idles at 800 rpm. At night in traffic the loads total 85 A. Using the characteristic curve, explain why the battery discharges at idle, find the deficit and the engine speed that removes it, and the effect of changing the pulley ratio to 3.0.
outline: Shape of the curve: zero below n₀, steep rise, self-limiting flat top; four marked speeds
I_max from the rated point
Current at idle and battery deficit; charge lost in 30 min
Engine speed for 85 A
Pulley ratio 3.0: new idle current
Field current and regulator act only below the curve
answer: Curve: at constant voltage and full field, output current is zero below the zero-ampere speed n₀, rises steeply, then flattens. The flattening is not the regulator: the emf E and the stator reactance X both grow in proportion to speed, so I ≈ (E − V) ÷ X tends to a limit, I ≈ I_max(1 − n₀ ÷ n). The speeds marked on the curve are n₀, the idle speed, the rated speed of 6000 rpm and the maximum speed.

answer.text: I_max from the rated point:
answer.pre: 120 = I<sub>max</sub>(1 − 1000 ÷ 6000) = 0.8333 I<sub>max</sub>  →  I<sub>max</sub> = 144 A

answer.text: Idle:
answer.pre:
N<sub>alt</sub> = 800 × 2.5 = 2000 rpm
I = 144 × (1 − 1000 ÷ 2000) = 72 A
deficit = 85 − 72 = 13 A, supplied by the battery
charge lost in 30 min of traffic = 13 × 0.5 = 6.5 Ah

answer: So the battery discharges at idle because the load (85 A) is above the curve at the idle speed (72 A); the regulator is already at full field and can do nothing more. Only speed raises the available current.

answer.text: Speed that removes the deficit:
Pulley ratio 3.0:

answer: The larger ratio almost closes the gap at idle; the limit on the ratio is the alternator's maximum permitted speed at the engine's top speed, so a ratio cannot be raised without checking that end.

answer.text: Summary of the cases:

answer: Sketch the curve with the 85 A load line: it crosses the curve at 2441 rpm; to the left the battery supplies the difference, to the right the regulator cuts the field to hold the set voltage. Check: at 6000 rpm the alternator gives 120 A, the rated value, so the model is consistent with its data.

bank.q: Explain how an electronic voltage regulator holds the bus voltage when speed and load change. The field winding is 3.0 Ω and the bus is held at 14.2 V. Find the PWM duty cycle for field currents of 4.0 A (heavy load) and 1.5 A (light load), and list the regulator versions.
outline: Sense, compare with reference, switch field; PWM; freewheeling diode
Average field current I_f = D × V ÷ R_f; duty-cycle calculation
Response to load on and to speed up
Temperature compensation, overvoltage protection, load-response function
Versions: contact, hybrid, discrete electronic, monolithic, multifunction/LIN
answer: Parts of an electronic regulator: a voltage divider senses the bus (or battery) voltage; a Zener diode or bandgap reference gives the set point; a comparator compares them; a driver transistor switches the field winding to ground (or supply); a freewheeling diode across the field carries its current while the transistor is off.

Action: if the sensed voltage is below the set point, the transistor turns on and field current rises; above it, the transistor turns off and the current decays through the freewheeling diode. The field inductance smooths the current, so the switching gives a steady average, set by the duty cycle D = t_on ÷ (t_on + t_off).

answer.text: Duty cycle from I_f = D × V_bus ÷ R_f:
answer.pre:
heavy load, 4.0 A:  D = I<sub>f</sub> R<sub>f</sub> ÷ V = 4.0 × 3.0 ÷ 14.2 = 0.845
light load, 1.5 A:  D = 1.5 × 3.0 ÷ 14.2 = 0.317
full field (D = 1):  I<sub>f</sub> = 14.2 ÷ 3.0 = 4.73 A

answer: Load switched on (headlamps): the bus dips, the comparator raises D (here from 0.317 towards 0.845), the field and output rise and the voltage returns to the set point. If D reaches 1 and the voltage is still low, the alternator is at its curve limit (typical at idle) and the battery supplies the rest.
Speed raised at constant load: the same field gives more emf, so the voltage starts to rise and the regulator lowers D. Speed never raises the regulated voltage; it only raises the available current.

Extra functions: temperature compensation lowers the set point when the battery is hot and raises it when cold, to avoid gassing or undercharging; overvoltage protection switches off the field if sensing fails; the load-response function ramps the field slowly when a big load switches on, so the engine idle does not dip.

answer.text: Regulator versions:

head: Version
How it switches the field
rows: a voltage coil opens and closes a contact
transistors, Zener reference on a board
one chip on the brush holder inside the alternator
IC with load response; ECU sets the voltage over LIN

answer: Sketch: divider → comparator (with reference) → driver transistor → field winding with freewheeling diode, and a PWM waveform with D = 0.845. Check: 4.0 A needs D = 0.845 < 1, so the field can still be raised to 4.73 A before the regulator runs out of control range.

bank.q: Draw the control circuit and the power circuit of a pre-engaged starter. Explain the roles of the pull-in and hold-in coils with their currents, and explain how the pre-engaged drive avoids the tooth clash of an inertia (Bendix) drive.
outline: Power: battery → heavy cable (30) → main contacts → motor → ground, 150–400 A
Control: key 50 → relay coil (0.1–0.3 A) → relay contact → neutral switch → terminal 50 → solenoid coils
Pull-in and hold-in together about 40 A, then hold-in about 10 A after the contacts short the pull-in coil
Pull-in coil feeds the motor slowly while meshing
Bendix: meshes by inertia while spinning, clash possible; pre-engaged meshes first
answer: Power circuit: battery positive → heavy cable (terminal 30, 16–50 mm²) → solenoid main contacts → motor terminal → series field and armature → ground → battery negative. It carries 150 to 400 A while cranking; in the chapter example 250 A.

Control circuit: battery → ignition switch in START (terminal 50 of the switch) → starter relay coil (0.1–0.3 A) → ground. The relay contact, fed from terminal 30, sends current through the neutral or clutch safety switch (and any immobiliser contact) to terminal 50 of the solenoid.

answer.text: Solenoid coils: both coils are fed from terminal 50. The pull-in coil (heavy wire) goes to the motor terminal; the hold-in coil (finer wire) goes to ground.
answer.pre:
pull-in about 30 A → resistance about 12 ÷ 30 = 0.4 Ω
hold-in about 10 A → resistance about 12 ÷ 10 = 1.2 Ω
while the plunger moves: 30 + 10 = 40 A in the terminal 50 line
after the main contacts close: 10 A

answer: Sequence: (1) key to START, relay closes; (2) both coils pull the plunger, which swings the lever and pushes the pinion towards the ring gear; the pull-in current also flows through the motor, so the armature turns slowly and the teeth find their gaps; (3) at the end of the stroke the main contacts close; both ends of the pull-in coil are now at battery voltage, so it carries no current, and the hold-in coil alone keeps the plunger in; (4) the motor cranks with 250 A; (5) the engine fires, the overrunning clutch lets the pinion overrun; (6) key released, the solenoid drops out and the spring returns the pinion.

Why two coils: a strong pull is needed only to move the plunger and lever; holding it needs much less force. Dropping from 40 A to 10 A cuts the coil heating from about 12 × 40 = 480 W to 120 W during cranking.

Inertia (Bendix) drive: the pinion sits on a coarse helical thread on the armature shaft. When full power is applied the armature spins, the pinion lags by its inertia and screws forward into mesh while turning; if a pinion tooth meets a ring-gear tooth they clash, wearing both. When the engine fires, it throws the pinion back.

answer.text: Comparison:

head: Feature
Inertia (Bendix)
Pre-engaged
rows: by inertia while spinning at full power
by solenoid lever before the main contacts close
none: motor only turns slowly during meshing
relay, solenoid with two coils, terminal 50

answer: Sketch both circuits with the four currents written on them: relay coil 0.2 A, solenoid 40 A then 10 A, motor 250 A. Check: the key switch never carries more than the relay current, so it does not burn.

bank.q: A fuel pump draws 8 A. It is 4.5 m from the relay and has its own return wire of the same length. The permitted voltage drop is 0.5 V and copper resistivity is 0.0172 Ω·mm²/m at 20 °C. (a) Size the wire. (b) Check it when the harness runs at 60 °C (resistivity +0.4 % per K). (c) Choose the fuse for a wire rated 20 A. (d) The car then stands for 21 days with a 25 mA standby current; find the charge lost from a 60 Ah battery.
outline: Three tests for a wire: voltage drop, temperature, strength
A = Iρl ÷ ΔU with l = 2 × 4.5 m because of the return wire
Hot resistivity and recheck; next size
Fuse between 1.25 × load and wire rating
Standby charge Q = I × t
answer: A wire must pass three tests: the voltage drop at full load within the permitted value, the conductor temperature within the insulation limit, and mechanical strength. Here the voltage drop and the temperature effect decide.

answer.text: (a) The pump has its own return wire, so the current flows out and back: l = 2 × 4.5 = 9.0 m.
answer.pre:
A = I × ρ × l ÷ ΔU = 8 × 0.0172 × 9.0 ÷ 0.5 = 2.48 mm²
next standard size: 2.5 mm²
drop at 20 °C = 8 × 0.0172 × 9.0 ÷ 2.5 = 0.495 V   (just inside 0.5 V)

answer.text: (b) At 60 °C the resistivity is 40 K × 0.4 % = 16 % higher:

answer: So a wire that passes at 20 °C fails in a hot engine bay; choose 4 mm² for the feed and return. A pump that receives 0.575 V less runs slower and delivers less fuel pressure, which shows up as hesitation under load.

answer.text: (c) Fuse: at least 25 % above the load so it does not blow in service, and not above the 20 A the wire can carry.
answer.pre:
lowest rating = 1.25 × 8 = 10 A
standard ratings: 5, 7.5, 10, 15, 20 A
choose 10 A (≤ 20 A wire rating)

answer: A 10 A fuse protects the 4 mm² wire with a wide margin; a 30 A fuse would let a short circuit overheat the wire before blowing, because the fuse must follow the wire, not only the load.

answer.text: (d) Standby discharge:
answer.pre:
t = 21 days × 24 h = 504 h
Q = 0.025 A × 504 h = 12.6 Ah
share of 60 Ah = 12.6 ÷ 60 = 21 %, so 79 % remains

answer: The battery still starts the car, but a few more weeks, or a cold morning, would not leave enough; long-parked vehicles need a maintenance charger or an isolator switch.

Sketch the circuit: terminal 30 → fuse 10 A → relay contact 30-87 → 4 mm² feed 4.5 m → pump → 4 mm² return 4.5 m → ground 31. Check: the hot drop on the chosen wire, 0.36 V, is well inside the 0.5 V limit, and the fuse (10 A) sits between the load (8 A) and the wire rating (20 A).

bank.q: A car cranks slowly on a cold morning. The battery rests at 12.3 V; the hydrometer reads 1.24, 1.24, 1.23, 1.12, 1.24 and 1.24 in the six cells; while cranking at 200 A the drop along the positive cable is 0.9 V. Using battery ratings, battery tests and starter circuit facts, locate the faults and justify each step.
outline: Observe symptoms: slow crank, dim lamps, solenoid click
Rest voltage and SG per cell; one weak cell
Load or conductance test against CCA
Voltage-drop test of cables and grounds; compare with expected resistance
Charging system check; decide what to replace
answer: Observe first: slow cranking with lamps that dim heavily points to a weak battery or high resistance in the high-current path; a single click with no crank points to the solenoid or a very high resistance; normal lamps and a slow crank point to the starter or engine. Here the crank is slow and cold, so test the battery, then the cables, then the starter.

answer.text: Rest voltage: 12.3 V after rest. Using the chapter scale (12.6–12.8 V full, about 12.2 V half, about 12.0 V a quarter), the battery is a little above half charge. Specific gravity per cell:

answer: Five cells agree within 0.01; cell 4 is 0.12 lower. Charging cannot cure a cell that stays far below the others, so cell 4 is faulty (sulfated, shorted or with shed material). Check against the rest voltage: 2.08 × 5 + 1.96 = 12.36 V, which matches the 12.3 V measured.

Load or conductance test: a battery with one weak cell fails the load test (half the CCA for 15 s, at least 9.6 V) because that cell's voltage collapses under current. In the chapter example a healthy battery of CCA 450 A fell to 10.1 V (11.1 mΩ) and a weak one to 9.2 V (15.1 mΩ). Expect the second result here; the battery needs replacing.

answer.text: Voltage-drop test on the positive cable at 200 A: the measured 0.9 V gives the resistance; compare with a new 16 mm² cable 1.0 m long.
answer.pre:
measured R = 0.9 V ÷ 200 A = 0.0045 Ω = 4.5 mΩ
new cable R = 0.0172 × 1.0 ÷ 16 = 0.00108 Ω → drop = 200 × 0.00108 = 0.22 V
excess = 4.5 − 1.1 = 3.4 mΩ, about four times the cable itself

answer: The extra 3.4 mΩ is almost certainly a corroded terminal or a loose clamp: clean and tighten, then repeat. Test the ground side the same way (battery negative to engine block, engine to body); the drop there should also be only a few tenths of a volt.

Effect on cranking: the starter sees the battery terminal voltage minus 0.9 V. With a weak cell and a corroded terminal both lowering the voltage, the starter torque curve drops and the stable cranking point moves to a lower speed, below the minimum starting speed on a cold morning.
Charging system: after fixing, check the bus at fast idle (13.8–14.4 V). A battery left at half charge in winter suggests short trips or a weak charging system, which would bring the fault back.

Decision: replace the battery (cell 4) with one of at least the original CCA and the same technology, clean and retighten the positive terminal, and confirm with a cranking voltage test. Check: each fault was found with a number (SG spread 0.12, 4.5 mΩ against 1.1 mΩ), not a guess.

bank.q: An alternator delivers 70 A at 14.0 V with 1300 W input at the pulley. The field is 4.0 A in 3.0 Ω, each stator phase is 0.007 Ω carrying 0.816 × I_dc RMS, and each diode drops 0.9 V. Analyse the power losses, find the efficiency and explain how losses and the machine itself limit output at low engine speed.
outline: Output and total loss; efficiency
Field and stator copper loss; diode loss 2V_F I_dc
Remainder: iron, brush, bearing, fan
How each loss varies with load and speed
Low speed: reactance curve, cooling and diode heating

answer.text: Output and efficiency:
Individual losses:
answer.pre:
field copper   = I<sub>f</sub>² R<sub>f</sub> = 4.0² × 3.0 = 48 W
stator copper  = 3 × (0.816 × 70)² × 0.007 = 3 × 57.1² × 0.007 = 68.5 W
diodes         = 2 × 0.9 × 70 = 126 W
sum            = 242.5 W
remainder      = 320 − 242.5 = 77.5 W (iron, brush, bearing, fan)

answer.text: Loss budget:

answer: The diodes are the largest single loss, because two always conduct and each drops about 0.9 V whatever the voltage; at a 14 V output, 1.8 V is about 11 % of the generated DC. This is why the rectifier sits on a heat sink in the air stream and why Zener or low-loss diodes matter.

Copper losses rise with the square of current, so they dominate at full load; iron loss rises with frequency (speed), and fan and bearing losses rise steeply with speed, so efficiency falls again at very high speed even though output is near its limit.

Low engine speed: the available output follows I ≈ I_max(1 − n₀ ÷ n). At idle the alternator is low on its curve (in the chapter example 72 A at 2000 rpm against 120 A at 6000 rpm), the regulator is already at full field (field copper loss at its maximum), and the fan, which turns with the rotor, moves less air while the diodes and windings still carry high current. Heat therefore limits how long the alternator can deliver its idle maximum.

Effect on the vehicle: when the loads exceed the curve at idle the battery supplies the difference; raising idle speed or the pulley ratio moves the operating point up the curve, while reducing losses (better diodes, liquid cooling) lets the same machine deliver more at idle without overheating.
Check: 48 + 68.5 + 126 + 77.5 = 320 W, and 980 + 320 = 1300 W, so the budget closes. The field duty cycle for 4.0 A is 4.0 × 3.0 ÷ 14.0 = 0.857, so the regulator still has a margin.

bank.q: Explain the structure of vehicle power distribution, the ignition high-voltage circuit and its distribution, and the EV traction domain. Justify fuses, relays and pre-charge with numbers: a 15 A heater on a 20 A wire, an ignition coil of ratio 100:1 interrupted at 350 V, and an inverter of 1 mF on a 400 V battery with a 50 Ω pre-charge resistor.
outline: 12 V tree: battery, main fuse, distribution box, fuses, relays, loads, ground
Fuse choice: above load, at or below wire
Relay: small control current switches large load
Ignition: coil primary/secondary, 35 kV ideal, breakdown 8 kV, distributor or COP, suppression
EV: 400 V battery, contactors, pre-charge (τ, peak current), isolation, DC-DC
answer: 12 V distribution: battery positive → main fuse or fusible link near the battery (protects the heavy cable, the most dangerous short in the car) → power distribution boxes under the bonnet and in the cabin → branch fuses → relays or switches → loads → body ground → battery negative. ECUs sit on fused branches; smart distribution replaces some fuses and relays with semiconductor switches that measure current.

answer.text: Fuse for the heater: the fuse protects the wire.
answer.pre:
lowest rating = 1.25 × 15 A = 18.75 A → standard 20 A
20 A ≤ wire rating 20 A → protected
with a 30 A fuse, a 28 A fault never blows it and the wire overheats

answer: Relay: the dash switch carries only the relay coil current (about 0.1–0.2 A), while the relay contact carries the heater's 15 A through short, heavy wires; the switch stays small and cool and the heavy wire runs the shortest route.

answer.text: Ignition high-voltage circuit: interrupting the primary current makes the field collapse and induce a high voltage in the many-turn secondary.
answer.pre:
ideal peak V<sub>s</sub> = V<sub>p</sub> × N<sub>s</sub>/N<sub>p</sub> = 350 × 100 = 35 kV
plug breakdown = 8 kV → voltage then falls to the arc voltage (a few hundred volts)
reserve (headroom) = 35 − 8 = 27 kV for worn or wide gaps

answer: Distribution of the high voltage: in older engines the distributor rotor, turning at half crankshaft speed, passes the pulse across a gap to each cap segment and HT lead in firing order; distributorless systems use one coil per pair of cylinders; coil-on-plug puts a coil on each plug. Resistor plugs and suppression leads slow the spark current pulse to cut radio interference.

answer.text: EV traction domain: a battery of about 400 V connects through contactors to the inverter, whose input capacitors are uncharged at start-up. Closing the main contactor directly would short them through a few tens of milliohms; a pre-charge resistor fills them first.
answer.pre:
without pre-charge, with 0.02 Ω in the loop: peak ≈ 400 ÷ 0.02 = 20,000 A
with 50 Ω: peak = 400 ÷ 50 = 8 A
time constant τ = RC = 50 × 0.001 = 0.05 s; 95 % charged after 3τ = 0.15 s
energy stored in the capacitors = ½CV² = 0.5 × 0.001 × 400² = 80 J

answer: Sequence: check isolation (isolation monitor), close the negative contactor and the pre-charge contactor, wait about 3τ until the capacitor voltage is near the battery voltage, close the main positive contactor, open the pre-charge path. Orange cables, a service disconnect and an interlock loop protect technicians; a DC-DC converter feeds the vehicle's own 12 V bus.

Evaluation: the three domains differ by orders of magnitude (14 V, 400 V, 35 kV) and must never be mixed; fuses, relays and pre-charge each protect a specific weak point: the wire, the switch and the contactor. Check: the pre-charge peak of 8 A is 2500 times smaller than the 20,000 A that would weld the contacts.

bank.q: Choose a battery, a starter and the starter cable for a petrol engine that needs 45 N·m at 200 rpm on the coldest morning. Assume the starter and its gears are 50 % efficient, the starter needs at least 9.6 V at its terminals, the cable and ground total 2 mΩ, the cold battery emf is 12.4 V, and (as a rough model) a battery's internal resistance is about (12.4 − 7.2) ÷ CCA. Justify each choice.
outline: Cranking power from torque and speed
Electrical input and current at 9.6 V
Allowed battery internal resistance → minimum CCA; choose rating; Ah and RC for loads
Starter type (gear reduction) and ratio
Cable size for a 0.25 V drop on 1.5 m
Charging check and assumptions

answer.text: Cranking power needed at the crankshaft:
Electrical input and current at the starter:
Battery: at 196 A the cable and ground drop 196 × 0.002 = 0.39 V, so the battery terminals must hold at least 9.6 + 0.39 = 9.99 V.
answer.pre:
allowed R<sub>int</sub> = (12.4 − 9.99) ÷ 196 = 0.0123 Ω = 12.3 mΩ
rough model R<sub>int</sub> ≈ 5.2 ÷ CCA → CCA ≥ 5.2 ÷ 0.0123 = 424 A
choose a standard battery with CCA 450 A

answer: Capacity: 450 A CCA batteries for cars are commonly about 60 Ah with a reserve capacity near 100 min; that gives the parked-car margin (21 days at 25 mA uses only 12.6 Ah, 21 %) and keeps the lights and ignition running for over an hour and a half at 25 A if the alternator fails. One 2 s crank uses only 196 × 2 ÷ 3600 = 0.11 Ah, so starting is a current problem, not a capacity problem.

Battery type: a maintenance-free (lead-calcium) flooded battery for a normal car; EFB or AGM if the car has start-stop, because it will be cycled far more often. For a cold region, the CCA, not the Ah, is the deciding number.

answer.text: Starter: a permanent-magnet gear-reduction starter gives the torque from a small, fast armature. With the chapter's gearing (planetary 4.5:1, pinion 10 and ring gear 130 teeth):
answer.pre:
overall ratio = 4.5 × 130 ÷ 10 = 58.5
armature speed for 200 rpm = 200 × 58.5 = 11,700 rpm
armature torque = 45 ÷ (58.5 × 0.9) = 0.85 N·m

answer: That armature speed is high; a slightly smaller ratio (for example a 3.5:1 planetary, overall 45.5, armature 9100 rpm, 1.10 N·m) suits a typical motor better. The pre-engaged drive with an overrunning clutch is chosen so the pinion meshes before full power and cannot be driven by the engine.

answer.text: Starter cable, 1.5 m, permitted drop 0.25 V:

answer: The chosen cable drops 0.20 V, inside the 0.39 V allowed for cable and ground together, leaving the rest for the ground strap and terminals, which must be clean.

Charging check: the alternator must recover the start charge and the standby losses; with a 120 A alternator and an idle current near 72 A (as in the alternator chapter), the recharge after a start takes seconds. Assumptions: the torque figure is a mean value (peak compression torque is higher), the 50 % efficiency includes motor and gears, and the CCA model is rough, so a margin (450 A against 424 A) is kept.

answer.text: Selection summary:

head: Item
Choice
Reason
rows: 12 V, CCA 450 A, about 60 Ah, RC about 100 min
R<sub>int</sub> ≤ 12.3 mΩ; standby and reserve margin
PM gear reduction, pre-engaged, about 1.9 kW input
942 W at the crank at 50 % efficiency

answer: Check: 9.99 V at the battery − 0.39 V in the cables = 9.6 V at the starter, as required, and 9.6 V × 196 A = 1882 W ≈ the 1885 W needed.

glossary.def: A rechargeable cell with a lead dioxide positive plate, a spongy lead negative plate and dilute sulfuric acid, giving about 2.1 V.
The lead-alloy frame that holds the active material and carries current to the plate lug.
A thin porous sheet between plates that stops them touching while letting ions pass.
Splitting of water into hydrogen and oxygen when a cell is pushed above about 2.3–2.4 V on charge.
Hard lead sulfate that forms on plates left discharged and no longer converts back on charge.
A float-type tester that reads electrolyte specific gravity to show state of charge.
A test at half the CCA for 15 s; a good battery stays above about 9.6 V.
A quick test that injects a small AC signal to estimate available CCA without discharging the battery.
A valve-regulated lead-acid battery whose acid is held in glass mats; oxygen recombines inside, so it loses almost no water.
Charge put into the battery minus charge taken out over a trip.
Ground: the return to battery negative through the body or a ground wire.
A drawing that shows how a circuit works, with current paths drawn straight from supply to ground.
A voltage surge on the bus when the battery is disconnected while the alternator is charging.
The route by which interference reaches a victim: conducted, capacitive, inductive or radiated.
A diode across a coil that carries its current at switch-off and clamps the voltage spike.
A belt-driven three-phase generator with a rotating field and stationary stator, rectified to DC by diodes.
A rotor with one field coil enclosed by two interlocking claw pieces that form alternate north and south poles.
The stationary laminated core with three windings in which the alternating emf is induced.
Three small diodes that feed D+ and the field from the stator once the alternator runs.
A rotating ring that, with a brush, feeds field current into the rotor.
The DC through the rotor winding; more field current gives more output voltage.
The fraction of each switching period that the regulator keeps the field switched on.
A short-duty DC motor that cranks the engine through a pinion on the flywheel ring gear.
An electromagnet with a plunger that moves the starter drive and closes the main contacts.
The small gear on the starter that meshes with the engine's ring gear.
Turning the engine at starting speed with the starter before combustion can sustain it.
An electromagnetic switch that lets a small control current switch a heavy load current.
A calibrated metal link that melts when current stays above its rating, protecting the wire.
The high-voltage winding and circuit of the ignition coil that fires the spark plug.
A heavy relay built to switch high current at high voltage, as in an EV traction circuit.
